content: Your doctor has prescribed heparin, a medication designed to thin your blood. This is intended to prevent the formation of blood clots in your body. Additionally, heparin may be used to stop existing blood clots from growing larger. The medication will be administered either intravenously (into a vein) or subcutaneously (under the skin). Your doctor will determine the most appropriate dosing schedule for your specific condition. Intravenous administration may last for 1 to 2 weeks, while subcutaneous injections could continue for up to 6 weeks or even 6 months. Heparin may also be prescribed for other medical purposes; consult your doctor or pharmacist for further details. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness and potential side effects of the treatment through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your body responds to the medication. Before starting heparin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to heparin, pork products, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and non-prescription medications you are currently taking, especially aspirin, ibuprofen (Motrin), headache or pain medications, naproxen (Anaprox, Aleve), and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney disease or diabetes. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. Should you become pregnant while on heparin, contact your doctor immediately. Before administering heparin, carefully inspect the solution. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or examine the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it appears discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution, but show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. If this occurs, contact your provider immediately to ensure your therapy can continue without interruption. Heparin may cause side effects, the most common of which is excessive bleeding (hemorrhage). If you experience any of the following symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately: bleeding from the gums or nose, unusually heavy menstrual bleeding, excessive bleeding from cuts or wounds, easy bruising, purplish areas on the skin, blood in your urine or stools, vomiting or coughing up blood, chills, fever, itching, or rash. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Your healthcare provider will likely provide you with a supply of heparin for several days. You will be instructed to store it in a cool, clean, and dry area. Do not allow the medication to freeze. Follow the storage instructions provided by your healthcare provider. Ensure you understand how to store the medication properly. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and store all medications and supplies out of the reach of children. Your healthcare provider will explain how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving heparin through a vein or under your skin, it is important to recognize the symptoms of a catheter-related infection (an infection at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin).
